ideas.notes: The product in three words: a hive, a memory and a mandate. Ruflo gives the many hands, an sgit vault the memory the client keeps, an Agent Behaviour Policy each role's mandate. In the first proof of concept the same eleven actions went through the policy engine in enforce mode and six were stopped: four denied, two sent to a person. Read through the Agent Behaviour Policy, a desktop is the agent's grant (everything it can reach) and the task is its mandate; the desktop's job is to keep the first close to the second and leave a footprint that can be read afterwards. That gives nine properties, and the design that follows writes one mandate per task before the desktop exists (what it is for, the hosts it may reach, the secrets it may use and for which hosts, the identity, how long), configures the desktop from it so the grant cannot drift past it by accident, and keeps a vault outside every desktop that it can append to and cannot rewrite. The four objects as the article tables them: mandate (elicited from business and user stories, locked under change control), grant or reach (measured, calibrated against logs), delta (reach minus mandate, derived and never authored) and barriers (none, expectation, setting, boundary; only a boundary is a control). The goal of every engagement is the smallest mandate, the smallest reach, the smallest gap. Self-policing is the fallback, not the goal: the value is in the act of creating the policy, which discovers what is actually possible. Reality is the calibrator: the documentation said an agent could not attach a file to an email, and Claude found a way. Anthropic's own words for why a rule in a prompt is hope: CLAUDE.md files are treated 'as context, not enforced configuration. To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a PreToolUse hook instead', and Claude Code's permission rules 'are enforced by Claude Code, not by the model'. Both modes of reaching a model (the API, where we write the whole system prompt, and the apps and Claude Code, where the vendor's prompt comes first) carry the policy as text the model is asked to keep. Hope or enforcement measured the share of a policy resting on hope falling from 97% to 23% with the right design. The one-sentence test for the barrier column: 'A control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include.' Atlassian's Rovo walked through as the shape of enterprise oversharing: nobody's permissions changed, what changed is that everything they already allowed is now one question away, and who the agent runs as (the person asking, the automation's connection account, or the agent's own account) decides the grant. The Northstar refund as why a behaviour policy is not enough: allowed to refund up to $200, owed $120, paid $150, and every control passes; a decision policy and a workflow policy answer 'who decides' and 'in what order'. The Northstar figures are a scripted simulation, no model called.

ideas.notes: The fork as the investor's insurance in place of control: 'A competitor who forks our code today gets our position as of today. They do not get our velocity.' Two conditions make it real: a genuinely open licence, not open core, and a copyright structure not gathered in one corporate holder (every catalogued relicensing between 2018 and 2024 was by a single corporate copyright holder). The fork disciplines the founder because it is possible and protects the founder because it is slow. Relicensing has a pattern: HashiCorp, Elastic and Redis each moved from an open licence to a source-available one, each produced a well-funded fork backed by the cloud providers it targeted (OpenTofu, OpenSearch, Valkey), and two of the three have since added an open licence back. Docker Desktop's paid tier for larger companies (August 2021) worked commercially, with annual recurring revenue past $50 million within months, and the alternatives grew: OrbStack, Colima, Podman Desktop and Rancher Desktop together are about 47% of the five tools' installs through Homebrew over the past year, a figure the article says overstates them. The buyer's side of the same protection: if the only people who can fix a tool are one partner's engineers, the company has swapped a deployment gap for a dependency. With the code open and the record kept, 'who will fix it?' has many answers: your team, the partner, another partner, or the agents, under a mandate, reading the record. ideas.notes: Costs for a newcomer is still a gap. The four properties serverless always meant to Dinis: it scales to zero, it costs little or nothing when it is not there, it starts fast, and it turns a capability into a commodity. The three words of the name each cover a part the others miss: ephemeral (comes and goes with use, costs nothing when gone), town planner (Wardley's word: mature, industrialised, a commodity, not a prototype held together behind the scenes), services (exposed for others to use, usually through the web). Lambda is an ephemeral town planner service sitting on town planner services like S3, which are always there. The name is a proposal; Dinis does not expect it to replace serverless. The free limits as Cloudflare's pages gave them on 18 October 2026 (they change): static assets free and unlimited on every plan; Workers 100,000 requests a day and 10 ms of CPU each, $5 a month for 10 million; R2 10 GB, a million writes and ten million reads a month, no egress fees, buckets pinnable to the EU; D1 5 GB; KV 100,000 reads and 1,000 writes a day; Durable Objects 100,000 requests a day and 5 GB; Workers AI 10,000 neurons a day then $0.011 per 1,000, 71 models on Cloudflare's own GPUs with a promise not to train on what you send; Email Routing free and unlimited; Access free to 50 users; domains at the registry's price. If staying inside is the point, the model name is the control: a @cf/ model stays on Cloudflare's GPUs, anything else leaves through AI Gateway. The catch for a non-specialist is setup, because Cloudflare's API cannot be called from a web page: a Deploy to Cloudflare button, a temporary account (live for an hour, since June), or an agent with the command line, once. Five packages, each the smallest set for one job and each on the free plan: a site on my domain; my vault, hosted; an assistant over my documents; an inbox that does things; a form or a small API. Each is a repository with a button, a skill and a page saying exactly what it can reach, which is its behaviour policy. ideas.notes: Answers the 2018 outline Serverless ('the path to Serverless', 'important to understand the limitations') from the other side: not Lambda, no back end at all. Not a claim that servers are bad: a trading system or a bank's ledger needs shared, live, authoritative state. The August 2026 precedent for the pattern, on sgit.ai: a static site on GitHub Pages has no server, no session and no place to keep a secret, so a chat box could not hold an API key; the answer was three tiers (a local matcher, the reader's own key, a vault bridge), with only the first free. The one real limit (a secret the reader must not hold cannot live in their browser) was met first here. The one real limit met by a product: a capped key per paying user is a secret the user may hold, and the provider's terms, not the architecture, are what stop it. Route 4, a metering proxy, is the smallest possible backend and still a backend: the audio passes through it, so custody, governance, scaling and on-call return and the privacy sentence on the home page has to change. It is also the only route that needs nobody's permission. The same constraint seen from sgit's side: a server that cannot read the data cannot do anything with it, so there is no server code, no deployment and nothing to patch; sgit's server is 'a dumb key-value blob store' and the deployment is the client. Features came from solving the problems the constraint created: clone --path holds only the folders you ask for and carries the rest by id, and with immutable encrypted objects a read is a plain GET, so any static host can serve a vault. Dinis names the temptation he has fallen for himself: a developer makes a change in the cheapest place with the fewest moving parts, which looks like the server until you have to maintain it. The list is the argument: a content site for several audiences where each part runs in the browser (personas opened from a published read key, a meter that charges by the share read and never blocks, a rating that sets the price, a newsroom of your own, SQL and SPARQL over the site's own data), with a 5 pound Stripe payment link and sign-in rented from companies whose product they are, and no account database, no session store, no API server. The lineage is local-first software (Ink and Switch, 2019: you should own your data in spite of the cloud); what vaults add is shared, persistent storage the operator cannot read, so client-side does not have to mean single-device. Next: a model in the client with the reader's own key, personas that follow the reader to every device, a signed receipt for payments, and the architecture packaged as a template another content site can start from. This last is what the weekend chapter would hand a founder.

ideas.statement: Most purchases are bets on future value, and the bet is often lost: gym members on a flat fee of over $70 attended 4.3 times a month and paid more than $17 a visit when a $10-a-visit pass was on offer. Turn it round where you can: start the user with credit, charge for the share they actually use, let the balance go negative, and ask for payment when the value is in view. A subscription is a discount for regular use, not rent on something somebody ignores; do not reach for one by default. The condition is a very large gap between the cost of serving and what you can charge, which a static site on a CDN has in the extreme and a business with a real cost per unit does not. ideas.title: We study survivors: a risky practice can look like the cause of success when only winners are counted
ideas.statement: Business writing looks at the winners, lists what they did, and says do the same; it almost never counts the people who did exactly the same and failed, or were never funded. Denrell showed in 2003 that risky practices unrelated to performance across everyone can look positively related to it in a sample of survivors. So the question is not what the winners did but why that one was chosen, funded and backed when others who did the same were not. Timing and place matter too: in MusicLab, showing popularity made success more unequal and less predictable, and the ten largest computer-science clusters hold 69% of US inventors in the field.

ideas.title: Investors select for the founder they can steer; control is written into the contract, and founders get replaced
ideas.statement: Dinis's hypothesis: between two founders with the same idea, drive and talent, one deciding factor is which one the investor believes they can control. The nearest tested trait is coachability, which investors openly prefer though 'being coachable doesn't necessarily make your firm more successful'. Control is in the paperwork: Kaplan and Strömberg found that when a firm performs poorly the investors obtain full control, and only when it performs very well do they give most of it back; non-compete and vesting terms make leaving expensive. Wasserman found 50% of founders no longer CEO by year three and fewer than 25% leading the IPO. The investors' answer is that control creates value (each level of founder control cut pre-money valuation by 17.1 to 22.0 percent), but that measures exits, not the mission; founder-led companies in the S&P 500 performed 3.1 times better in shareholder returns from 1990 to 2014. In Wardley terms the investor moves the founder towards commodity, as record labels did to performers once the songs, the producers and the distribution were the assets.

ideas.notes: The article's own limits: no study tests controllability directly; the value evidence cuts against the argument; Bain's figures are not peer-reviewed; the founder-tenure figures are from the late 1990s and early 2000s; not that investors are villains; and Dinis has a stake. The profile it says is filtered out is the founder with a strong vision and strong ethics, which it says is close to many European founders.

ideas.title: Sell, don't issue: the investor buys the founder's shares, the founder lends the company what it needs, and nobody buys the steering wheel
ideas.statement: For a founder who has already won (paying customers, profit, growth, more than one investor who wants in): instead of the company issuing new shares, the investor buys ordinary shares the founder already owns, in a private sale, so the founder is paid now for years of underpaid work, the company is not diluted, and no board seat, veto or liquidation preference comes with the money. If the company needs cash, the founder lends part of the proceeds back, subordinated by contract to every other creditor, at a modest fixed rate or none, repaid if the company succeeds. A founder lending their own money watches every penny, and 74% of high-growth internet startups fail from premature scaling. The investor's insurance is not control but the fork: with everything open source, if the founder goes wrong they can take the code and back a better service.

sources.where: Sell, don't issue; Lend, don't dilute; The open source safety valve; Why it could raise the odds; A worked example

ideas.notes: The worked example, illustrative: a UK company worth £10 million, £2 million invested, the founder keeps 80% either way; in the sale the founder pays about £420,000 in tax (18% on the first £1 million under Business Asset Disposal Relief from 6 April 2026, 24% above) and has about £1.58 million, lends £0.75 million and keeps about £0.83 million; the buyer pays 0.5% stamp duty. The article says no study tests the model, the fork as insurance is an argument not a tested mechanism, it is not tax or legal advice, and Dinis has a stake. The fork is slow both ways: three months at best, closer to a year, for an established company to reach where the original team is.

ideas.title: What breaks: EIS is lost on bought shares, a big early sale reads as doubt, the founder-lender is a creditor, and a broad non-compete closes the fork
ideas.statement: The model has costs a founder should know before the term sheet does. UK angels get EIS relief of 30% and SEIS of 50% only on newly issued shares, so bought shares are that much dearer to them; expect a lower price or a hybrid with some new shares. Common stock is often priced 10% to 30% below the last round. Balderton says it would not expect a founder to sell more than 10% at growth stage and has walked away over the size of a secondary. A founder who sells and lends back has moved part of their risk ahead of the new investors unless the loan is subordinated in writing. Control can return through a shareholders' agreement, and the model only holds if the founder refuses those terms. And refuse a broad non-compete: it keeps the fork for the investors and takes it from the founder; offer confidentiality, no poaching and no use of the brand instead.

sources.where: What breaks; When it works and when it does not

ideas.notes: Fits badly: deep tech, hardware, a land grab against funded rivals, proprietary code (no fork), investors whose model needs control rights. The UK figures are for 2026/27; the EY secondary pricing data is from Indian deals; the UK's 2023 plan to cap non-competes at three months was never legislated. Four fine-print points for a lawyer are in the article: transfer restrictions, selling above market value as employment income, success-linked interest treated as a distribution, and the order of issue and sale in a hybrid.

ideas.title: The expert founders, in numbers: 45 is the mean age, experience doubles the odds, a third of US startups have one founder
ideas.statement: In a study of 2.7 million US founders the mean age at founding of the 1-in-1,000 fastest-growing new ventures is 45.0, and founders with three or more years in the same industry reached top-tier growth at twice the rate of those with none. Carta: solo founders rose from 23.7% of new US startups in 2019 to 36.3% in the first half of 2025. Stripe: its top 100 AI companies reached $1 million in annualised revenue in a median of 11.5 months. The venture model behind the outsider playbook: in Horsley Bridge's data on just over 7,000 investments from 1985 to 2014, about half returned less than the original investment and 6% of deals produced 60% of total returns. The experts were never held back by knowledge; they were held back by access to capital, engineers and the long build before anything could be shown, which is the part that got cheap.

ideas.title: Europe's slower, sceptical money suits a founder who can build first
ideas.statement: European investors are said to want to see it working, and the data has a version of it: European companies raise at higher revenue (a median band of $1 million to $5 million against $100,000 to $1 million in the US), at lower pre-money valuations ($6.54 million against $14.64 million), with funding targets 46% smaller. That scepticism is what an expert founder now needs, because money too soon is one of the worst things that can happen: 74% of high-growth internet startups fail from premature scaling and investors put in 2 to 3 times more than needed in the discovery phase. Europe is weak at scaling (5% of global VC funds raised against 52% in the US; close to 30% of unicorns founded in Europe 2008 to 2021 moved abroad), and strong at the first part, which is the part that now matters most. Its values fit too: an open source strategy in the Commission's June 2026 sovereignty package, and impact at 15% of European VC against 7% in North America.

ideas.statement: The first commit was on 8 February 2026, with a spec that set the rule everything since has followed: files encrypted on the client, the key never sent. send.sgraph.ai was live on 13 February. The Stripe checkout went live on 1 March; on 2 March there were ten paying customers, recruited with an offer of £5 of credits and a £5 Amazon voucher, which several declined. The first feature request, a folder not a file, came the same day and was proposed at 20:26, implemented at 20:48 and given a viewer at 22:15. Taking it to market end to end is where Dinis learnt Stripe, pricing and the rest a real product needs, which paid off later in the newsroom.

ideas.title: The SaaS apocalypse will be decided by inertia, not by AI, because AI is available to both sides
ideas.statement: The incumbents have the same models the newcomers have, plus more data, more engineers and more money; if the technology decided this they would already have won, and two and a half years in they have not. What decides it is where a company sits on the evolution axis and how much past success it has to protect: Nokia met the mobile phone with nothing to protect and became the category, met the iPhone with fifteen years of success to protect and was gone from it within seven. Past success breeds inertia; new entrants, unencumbered by it, initiate the change. The newcomer was never on the rails, which is why the newcomers, not the incumbents, are the ones to watch.

ideas.title: Users were never happy: 91% frustrated, 80% of features rarely or never used, $21 million a year in idle licences
ideas.statement: Business software did 80% of what you needed and the remaining 20% was as painful as before you bought it, and it is measured: Freshworks found 91% of 8,698 people frustrated by inadequate workplace technology; Pendo found 80% of features in the average product rarely or never used, across 615 products; Zylo puts the average organisation's waste on unused licences at $21 million a year. 73% of companies prepare VAT returns in Excel and 78% of British companies say spreadsheets support key financial decisions: the persistence of Excel is the clearest evidence that SaaS failed them, because it is the one tool where they control the shape of the thing. You pay 100% for the 10% of features you actually wanted.

ideas.title: What SaaS refused to build to protect its moat is exactly what a customer's agent needs
ideas.statement: Portability, open schemas, a real API at the centre, data you can take out, capabilities you can call from outside: for twenty years these were treated as churn risks and starved. Now the customer's agent turns up wanting exactly that list and finds a product built to prevent it; the moat has become the thing the water cannot get past in either direction. Strip the interface and most of these companies are a database, a messaging system and a state machine, and that can be built, though it is hard to build well. A founder builds the list from the start.

ideas.title: A company sits in the two moves on the map: a guess becoming a product, and a product becoming a commodity
ideas.statement: Who reads the code depends on where it is on the map: explorer code is read for intent, mostly by agents; villager code is read line by line, because this is where changes land and the blast radius lives; town planner code is read by deterministic checks at the boundary, with a person for the exceptions. The company sits in the two moves between them: from explorer to villager, when a guess becomes a product and needs the review it never had; from villager to town planner, when a product becomes a commodity and the review becomes checks that run without anyone. The trap on both sides is not knowing which stage the code is at: teams find a model's mistakes too risky and swing to reviewing everything by hand.

ideas.notes: Quote, word for word, from the March 2026 article the newsroom cites: 'Before AI agents started writing code, you could argue that 90% of the code running in production was not being read by anyone.' The SaaS article's version: businesses that take the finished brief and run it, paid by consumption and by the fact that it keeps working, not by the seat; and 'more engineers, not fewer'. Extends the-handover from a frame about prototypes to a frame about where a company's value is.

ideas.title: A budget per step, declared before anything runs, is the objective way to say good enough; the five whys move it
ideas.statement: Agents keep going, that is what they do, and one agent handing work to another looks efficient while it spends. The way to stay on the right side of diminishing returns is a budget per altitude and per change, decided in advance, so a workflow's maximum cost is knowable before it runs rather than discovered afterwards; work handed from agent to agent carries its budget and never widens it. Being able to tell a team the budget is spent was one of the most useful controls Dinis ever had, because teams are very good at keeping going. Then the five whys: every finding at one layer is a question about the layer below, and the fix goes there as a rule, so the next change like it is caught for the price of a query. Onboard by starting at one point and continuing, never by analysing everything.

ideas.title: Send an agent, not a spreadsheet: due diligence derived from the code, not composed by the vendor
ideas.statement: Due diligence was a form because the alternative did not exist: the standard questionnaire has 627 questions, vendors answer 37.3 requests a month and spend 179 hours on them, and the answers are written by the people being asked. Now a buyer can send a prompt, or a small agent under a behaviour policy, to run inside the vendor's environment and come back with a graph of what is there: what reaches production that no person reviewed, whether the documentation matches the code, whether there is a threat model, what the last fifty bugs touched, which agents touch the pipeline and under what policy. The vendor reads what leaves and can redact but not rewrite, because the answer is derived, and companies will not put a false map on a record. A buyer asking costs nothing; a supplier not answering looks worse than one answering badly. Investors and acquirers get the same visibility in the same month.

ideas.notes: The agent does not exist yet; the article is the case for it. The regulation arrives before the visibility: the EU Product Liability Directive applies to products placed on the market from 9 December 2026 and presumes a product defective where the manufacturer fails to disclose relevant evidence. Placed in sell because it is what the founder's buyers will do to them.

ideas.title: A startup should double down on understandability: less code, the same tools, and it can be checked and pass
ideas.statement: The test is risk-based, not pure. A startup that says it generated most of its code fast, that the product is not mission-critical and here are the mitigations has passed; what fails is not knowing. So build the graph of your own repository, keep the threat model with the code, write a behaviour policy for every agent, trace bugs to changes, and answer the buyer's questions in the buyer's format before being asked. The startup can play the same game as the biggest buyer, with open source tools, and it has less code: understanding ten thousand lines is a week, ten million that nobody still at the company wrote is a programme. The incumbent's advantage was that nobody could check; the startup's is that it can be checked and pass.

ideas.notes: A threat model is the fastest read of a team's understanding: one that says 'we have a weakness here, exploiting it needs a nation-state, we will not defend against it' is a good one. The evidence that review is being skipped is dated in the article: AI accounts for 42% of committed code and only 48% always verify it (Sonar, January 2026); 80% of PRs have no human comment when an AI review tool is on (Qodo, 2025).

ideas.title: The agent behaviour policy is the due diligence document: a buyer reads the blast radius off it, and its absence says the most
ideas.statement: A behaviour policy, written before an agent's first run, says what the agent is, which identity it uses, what it may read, write, not do and spend, who approves what, which risks were accepted by whom and for how long, and where its actions are recorded. Read by a buyer it says something else: the worst case (a deploy agent whose identity has no merge right and no production credential can at most break staging), which controls are enforced by the identity and which are only instructions, and which risks the vendor accepted on the buyer's behalf. A vendor with agents in its pipeline and no policy to show has agents whose blast radius nobody has written down, which is a finding before any code is read.

ideas.title: Selling a service: each step small enough to say yes to, and each ends with something they keep
ideas.statement: The path for selling an agentic service: a free conversation about what the client wants agents to do and must never do; a first run on a real problem for £10 to £50 that leaves a vault; £500 for about two hours or £1,500 for a day to steer it or write the behaviour policy for one team; a four-day pilot in their own environment for £5,000; then a maintained setup from £149 a month so they run it themselves. The boutique benchmarks are the same shape everywhere: a free call, a paid discovery (a one-week audit at £2,500, a 14-day sprint at €2,900, a two-week assessment at $4,999), a fixed-price pilot (from £8,000), a build, a retainer. The prices are hypotheses to test with the first ten customers, and the plan says so: no paid run yet.

ideas.title: The market is crowded at the top and thin on evidence: sell the record the client keeps
ideas.statement: The large consultancies each have an agent platform, the model vendors sell through partners and their own engineers, and boutiques sell fixed-price pilots; what the people in between lack is not another platform but evidence they can inspect. Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027, citing escalating costs, unclear value and inadequate risk controls, and warns of agent washing. The position for a small seller is evidence first: every engagement leaves a vault the client keeps, with the work, the history and a ledger of what each agent did and was allowed to do. The demonstration is the sales process, and the demonstration is checkable.

ideas.notes: The demonstration: a talk built and run by a governed agent hive in about a day, 28 workers, 57 vault commits, no plaintext in anything the server stored, every vault deleted at the end; the runs were not gated by a compiled behaviour policy, which was shown separately. Dinis proposes 'agentics' as the word for what is sold: the practice, not one workflow.

ideas.title: A service only scales with people: a curated marketplace of consultants, joined by proof of work
ideas.statement: Agentic engagements need someone who knows the client's world and can steer a hive in it, and there are more of those people in a community than hours in a founder's week. So alongside the offers, a small curated list of consultants who deliver on the same stack, where the client picks the kind of project first and then the people. Joining copies the markets that work: apply, show proof of work (a public vault or repository of a real run with its ledger), peer review by two members, a thirty to forty-five minute interview with a scenario, a first engagement shadowed, and standards including a behaviour policy for consultants, the same idea applied to agents. The consultant sets the price within the band and keeps most of it; markets sit between 5% and 20% in total (Malt charges freelancers 5%, Upwork 0% to 15%, Braintrust 15% to the client).

ideas.title: Three honest tiers for a model on a site with no server: a local matcher, your own key, or a vault bridge
ideas.statement: A static site has no server, no session and no place to keep a secret, so the usual chat box (a backend holding the API key) is not an option. The honest choices are three: a deterministic matcher in the browser that is free, private, works offline and shows which words it matched on (the default, because a reader should never have to hold a credential to use an index); the reader's own key, opt-in and labelled, which lives in the page's origin and is a trust decision presented as one; and a vault bridge where the host holds the key below the permission floor and the app never sees it. When the model call fails, fall back to the first tier and say so.

The bridge's own qualification travels with it, quoted: 'The bridge protects your key; it is not yet a boundary that prevents all egress.' Only the first tier is free; the third was not built (on the board as T11).

It knows only the catalogue, nineteen theses and summaries quoted from each site's own words. For a founder shipping in a weekend, that is the discipline: the narrow thing that is right over the wide thing that drifts.

ideas.title: Billing by not building billing: the commercial model is a property of the key
ideas.statement: A user pays five pounds through a payment link; the company keeps its cut at the moment of payment; the rest becomes the credit limit on a key handed to the user; the provider meters it and the key stops when it is spent. Against a billing system (a meter on every call, a ledger per user, disputes, refunds, fraud, custody of the data while it meters) that is a payment, a cut, a key with a ceiling and nothing else, and it is more profitable per pound because the margin is taken once, up front. The minimum top-up is five pounds because a card fee with a fixed component makes a one-pound purchase return about 59 pence of inference.

ideas.notes: Could also sit in price-it-then-give-it-away. The model was written down on 28 July 2026, the day the product started, in a brief headed 'Billing by not building billing'. It is why a router like OpenRouter does well: it sells credit, keeps a margin and meters for everyone else. The user owns the ceiling: a key with a limit cannot cost more than the limit, and the user can revoke it at the provider in one click.

ideas.title: Twice now the product was possible and the licence was the blocker: read the terms, not only the docs

OpenRouter's Management API documents 'unique API keys for each customer instance' with credit limits, and section 7(4) of its terms (31 August 2026) forbids 'reselling API access to Models', so a plan built against the docs was dead on the page that documented it. Before a founder builds the commercial model on a provider, the terms are the thing to read, and an enterprise or OEM agreement is a door to ask about, not a feature to assume.

ideas.title: VoiceDebrief: a product with no server that shipped in three weeks and stopped at the one thing it could not sell
ideas.statement: VoiceDebrief.ai turns a voice note into a transcript, a translation and a debrief in the browser, on the user's own OpenRouter key, with no account, no server and nothing stored; a 42-second note costs about a third of a penny. Built in the open from 28 July 2026: 239 commits and 27 releases in the first three weeks, then eleven commits the week after, then three, and a last commit on 7 September. What stopped it was not a server but the lack of one: the capped key per user that the model needed is forbidden by the provider's terms, and the alternative, a metering proxy, is the backend the product exists to avoid.

ideas.notes: Dated 12 October 2026; Dinis says he is involved in VoiceDebrief and that the commit counts show when the work stopped, not why. The four routes: buy a capped OpenRouter key per user (forbidden by the standard terms); a provider that sells the capped key itself or lets it be issued under its terms (ElevenLabs the nearest fit, the gap is one sentence); bring your own key, kept (what runs today, honest, no margin, and the five minutes it takes to get a key is where most people stop); a metering proxy (the smallest backend, and a backend, custody and on-call return). The one part of the product with a server is the WhatsApp path, an n8n workflow behind a Cloudflare Worker. The method at the end is worth the book's attention: agents draft the letters to providers, Dinis sends, the ask is one sentence, and every answer is recorded as an issue with its date so the map is updated as a version rather than a new article.

ideas.title: Git for things you cannot put on GitHub: what an encrypted vault is
ideas.statement: There is a category of file with nowhere good to live: a risk register with real system names, an analysis still being argued about, the working memory of an agent that has read your codebase for a month, client material under NDA. It wants history, branches, diffs and a link, and it is the reason people say 'we can't put that in GitHub', so it ends up in a shared drive or a thread nobody can diff. sgit is git for those files: encrypted before they leave your machine, versioned like git, stored on a server that holds ciphertext and nothing else, not filenames, not directory structure, not commit messages. There is no key escrow, no admin override and no support engineer who can recover it, which is a feature with a real cost.

sources.where: the opening; The part that is easy to say and hard to build

ideas.notes: Dated 25 August 2026. The evidence in the article: an object is 786 bytes of AES-256-GCM ciphertext named by the SHA-256 of the encrypted bytes, so the host can deduplicate it, cache it and serve it from a CDN without knowing what it is; all nineteen published vaults cloned from their published keys, 1,389 files, no failures. Underneath it is real version control (multi-parent commits, a tree per directory, merge-base, three-way merge), not a sync folder. Status, plainly: sgit is beta and says so on every page; pip install sgit-ai, pure Python, two runtime dependencies, Apache-2.0. The then-and-now for the 2018 Backup your life: back up into a vault whose key you hold.

ideas.title: One string is address, authorisation and key; the read key derived from it is safe to publish
ideas.statement: A vault key is a passphrase and a vault id in one string, and it is three things at once: the address of the vault, the authorisation to write to it, and the key that decrypts it. Lose it and the data is gone; leak it and someone can rewrite your history. From it, one way, comes a read key: same vault, read-only, safe to publish, and the read key is the entire credential, with no account, no login and no access request. That asymmetry is the whole sharing model: every vault linked from sgit.ai is published as a read key, and no vault key has ever been published, a rule enforced by a tripwire in the release pipeline.

sources.where: The part that is easy to say and hard to build; Ten seconds of proof; Try it

ideas.notes: This site runs on the same rule: the public read key in admin/content/vault.json is the only key that belongs in the repository, and the gate refuses the private prefix (CLAUDE.md). The second article adds the other credentials that sit beside the vault key, each made for one job: a write key the server checks as a hash, an append token that writes one message to one lane and nothing else, and a PKI key pair (RSA-OAEP 4096 for encryption, ECDSA P-256 for signing). In the browser the key sits after the # in the URL, which browsers do not send to the server.

ideas.title: An app in a vault runs against the vault without ever being handed a key
ideas.statement: A vault can contain an application, not only documents, and the application runs against the vault without ever holding a credential: it declares permissions of nothing, the host reads the vault and passes results in, and the app never sees a key. Capability without credential means you can run code you did not write against data you care about, with the blast radius set by a config file you can read in one screen. The same shape holds for a model: the key lives below the permission floor, the host makes the call, and the app never sees it.

ideas.notes: Belongs beside mandate-reach-gap: the config file is the written reach, enforced by the host rather than hoped for in a prompt. The chat article's qualification applies: the bridge protects the key it was trusted with; it does not yet stop a malicious app calling a provider with a credential of its own.

ideas.title: Encryption on the client moves the problem from the data to the keys, and the sovereignty line to whoever holds them
ideas.statement: When the server can read what it stores, all of it has to be protected: every copy, backup, log and replica, and every person and process with access. When the server holds ciphertext named by the hash of that ciphertext, the problem moves to protecting the keys, which is much smaller, and the key becomes the whole question: where it is kept and how it travels decides who can read, who can write and what a leak costs. The sovereignty line stops being where the data is stored and becomes who holds the keys, so data can sit with a provider or in a country with sovereignty gaps and you remain sovereign over it and able to move it; the European Data Protection Board treats strong encryption with the keys retained solely by the exporter as an effective supplementary measure for transfers.

ideas.notes: The EDPB source is Recommendations 01/2020, version 2.0, 18 June 2021, use case 1, quoted in the article: 'the EDPB considers that the encryption performed provides an effective supplementary measure.' The same idea as sovereignty as the ability to move (hack-your-country). The cost of the design, from the keys article: everything that matters is in the key, which is why key management is where the effort goes now.

ideas.title: Where the keys live: a password manager for the keys a person holds, a registry vault for the keys agents make
ideas.statement: Once agents create vaults several times a day, keeping the keys by hand stops working. The keys a person holds go in a password manager, which is and will stay the preferred home; everything the agents create goes to a registry, a private vault run by its own isolated Claude session with no other access, the vault of vaults, so a key is never lost and never has to live in a browser tab or a chat. Remembering keys under aliases on one machine is a convenience, not a management system. The weakest step is giving a key to another agent, because the agent platforms have no secrets per session.

sources.where: Where the vault keys are kept today; The weakest step: giving a key to an agent; What comes next

ideas.notes: State at sgit-ai v0.20.0, 10 October 2026. The gap, quoted from the platform's docs: on Claude Code on the web an environment variable is one 'any command Claude runs can read' and 'Anyone who uses the environment can read the values'; a network secret keeps the key outside the VM but is per environment and cannot help with a vault key, because decryption happens inside the session; Codex removes its secrets before the agent phase starts. So a key for another agent travels in the prompt (a transcript), in an environment variable (every session reads it), or not at all, with the agent making its own vault and sending the key back on a lane, the pattern used most. The four tracks next: password manager integrations (an open call published, not followed up yet), secrets.sgit.ai (a keyring unlocked by a passkey's PRF output, a 128-bit recovery code shown once, at v0.1.13 the design and a lab shipped and the app proposed), PKI (RFC 0001), and decryption out of band (an idea, not a design).

ideas.title: A vault per conversation and per job: a leaked key exposes one small thing, not an inbox
ideas.statement: Working this way you start making very small vaults for very specific things: a communication vault for the two or three agents on a job, in which they talk and work through versioned, encrypted files. What an agent needs to join one is small: the vault key, sgit and network access to one host, or a server inside its own network. This is the right shape for security: a leaked key exposes one small vault and one conversation, not an inbox, a drive or an account, and every word is on the record for the person who holds the keys. It is also why the number of keys grew faster than one person could manage by hand.

sources.where: Small vaults for small jobs

ideas.notes: Pairs with an-agent-is-a-session-with-a-focus (one session per topic) and with the main workflow the article describes: give Claude no permissions and no access to anything, only the vault it uses to communicate, or a vault it creates and the person then captures. Inside the vaults the agents use EmailFS and IssuesFS, file-based protocols for mail and issues.

ideas.title: Append lanes: one POST from anywhere, readable only by the vault's owner
ideas.statement: A lane is a write-only channel attached to a vault. A sender holds a token for one lane and the owner's public key, seals its message to that key and sends it with a single POST; the owner decrypts with a private key that never leaves them, and the server keeps only hashes and ciphertext, so compromising it yields hashes and ciphertext. One lane per sender, so one can be revoked without touching the others. It is used for key handover, for logs and observations from sessions that hold no vault key, for what a reader fills in on a web page, and for messages between agents on different platforms with different owners. A little like email, and the token is still a secret: it cannot read, but with the vault id it authorises writes.

ideas.notes: This is the piece that lets a site with no server take input: the newsroom's newsletter sign-ups and shared reading go through the same encrypted, write-only inbox (no-server-by-design), and the agent desktop design sends outputs and the footprint to a vault the desktop can append to and cannot rewrite. The no-server article notes it is the one part of the vault server that needs a small piece of server logic.

ideas.title: Nobody buys it for the encryption: the features came from the constraint
ideas.statement: Encryption is an important property, not a reason to choose a tool, and leading with it was a mistake Dinis made himself: if sgit succeeds it will be because it has better features and better workflows. Many of those came from the encryption as a constraint, because innovation needs constraints and the loop of trying, failing and shipping; the research is more careful than the slogan, an inverted U-shaped effect, some constraint helps and too much hurts. The same applies to design: take things away until it hurts, and stop there; the best product is not the one you use because you have to but the one that hurts when you stop.

sources.where: The mistake I made first; Open source, as a constraint

ideas.notes: The research named is Acar, Tarakci and van Knippenberg, Creativity and innovation under constraints, Journal of Management, 2019, quoted: 'an inverted U-shaped effect of constraints on creativity and innovation'. Dinis declares a stake: sgit is his, and the article says the market will decide. A line for the cutter too: 'take things away until it hurts, and stop there, because past that point it gets worse.' Tension to watch with ship-now-ship-serverless, which presents SG/Send and sgit by their privacy property: the book should sell them by the workflow and name the privacy as the property.

ideas.title: Client-side encryption reduces the exposure under GDPR; it does not take you out of it
ideas.statement: Dinis's memo said that with the data encrypted you do not have to worry about GDPR, and the article corrects it: for whoever holds the keys, encrypted personal data is still personal data, storing it is still processing, and the controller's duties stay (the UK regulator says not to think encrypted data is outside the UK GDPR). What encryption does is reduce the exposure, and the law recognises it: Article 32 lists encryption as a security measure, and under Article 34(3)(a) a breach need not be communicated to the people affected if the data was made unintelligible to anyone not authorised, provided the key was not lost with it. The Court of Justice held in September 2025 that pseudonymised data is not personal data in all cases and for every person, which may help a store that never has the keys. Much less to worry about, not nothing.

ideas.notes: An instance of asked-to-be-corrected: the memo's claim stands corrected in the article, and the book must not repeat the memo. Sources named in the article: GDPR Articles 32 and 34; ICO encryption guidance; Court of Justice case C-413/23 P, press release of 4 September 2025. Not legal advice. Answers the 2018 outline GDPR, which the map says no article covered for developers.

ideas.title: Open source as a constraint: all of it, or it is an evaluation version with a better name
ideas.statement: The constraint is that there is no private code. It makes the code easy to deploy, run and change, including by the customer, which solves many sovereignty problems on its own, and it removes two temptations: to lock the customer in, and the curse of most startups, building every feature and integration one customer wants until the roadmap belongs to everyone but the startup. With open source the answer is: here is the code, integrate it yourself or pay us to do that specific thing. That is why you cannot open source half of it: a community edition that turns proprietary when you use it for real is an evaluation version, and Elastic, HashiCorp and Redis each moved to a non-open licence and each produced a well-funded fork (OpenSearch, OpenTofu, Valkey). The business model that follows is selling customisation and keeping it working.

sources.where: Open source, as a constraint; All of it, or it is an evaluation version; The business model that follows

ideas.notes: Distinct from the-fork-next-door (the fork as protection) and open-source-removes-the-moat-excuse (why it is easy to throw your own technology away): this is the founder's business reason for all of it. Elastic (29 August 2024) and Redis (1 May 2025) have since added an open licence back; the Open Source Initiative said the SSPL is not an open source licence (19 January 2021). The article's own limit: that small teams win this way is Dinis's view from what he sees, not a study. The constraints remove bad business decisions and leave the good one: if the code is open and the server holds nothing, you cannot sell access to the code or rent the data back.

ideas.title: The name shows the glue: a first version is often a villager's work dressed as a town planner's
ideas.statement: Naming a service as ephemeral, town planner and a service makes you ask whether it is really a commodity or only looks like one, and plenty of things sold as commodities are a large amount of custom technology glued together behind the scenes. Lambda, the definition of serverless for most people, ran on Linux containers inside EC2 instances for its first four years, until Firecracker replaced them from 2018, in its builders' own words. A per-hour bill for a 'serverless' product usually means the provider cannot yet spin the thing up and down fast and safely enough to bill by use: an engineering gap on their side, passed to you as a cost. Not a criticism, that is how services become commodities, and the floors that halve and the scale-to-zero that arrives are the record of it maturing in public.

Werner Vogels is quoted: AWS delivers 'new services often with a minimal feature set' and lets customers 'help drive the roadmap'. The Firecracker account is AWS's own (NSDI 2020). Wardley in 2016: 'It's not really serverless but more I don't care what a server is.'

ideas.title: Move the cloud, not the code: a twin the application cannot tell from the real service
ideas.statement: Workloads stay on hyperscalers because moving means changing code: every call to S3, EC2 and IAM is written into applications that work today and nobody wants to touch. So the requirement is that the application must not know it has moved. The same calls land on a twin, an open source interface to a real system valued for one thing, that the client cannot tell the difference, and the twin decides where the bytes go: real S3, an sgit vault, a European operator's data centre, a laptop. Switching a mock costs a code path; switching a twin costs an endpoint, so migration becomes a configuration decision rather than a project, and projects get cancelled. The S3 twin exists as open source; EC2 and IAM do not yet.

sources.where: Why workloads do not move; The criterion: the code must not know; This is not theoretical: the S3 twin

ideas.notes: Dated 12 October 2026, from a digital sovereignty event; the chief executive is not named and did not review it. AWS's European Sovereign Cloud went live on 15 January 2026, a separate cloud with its first region in Brandenburg, operated by EU residents; the article's reading: 'Sovereignty that depends on one company's API is sovereignty by permission.' None of it works if the twin layer is closed: swap one vendor's API for another vendor's proprietary wrapper and the lock-in has moved, not gone.

ideas.title: The reason to move is never sovereignty or cost: sell value that lands the day they switch
ideas.statement: Sovereignty and cost reduction are important and never urgent; they sit on the risk register under important, not urgent, and nobody signs the risk of a migration for a principle or for a return that depends on a future event. The person signing needs value that lands the day they switch and gives them cover if it goes wrong: backups that exist, every object version controlled, encryption the operator cannot read with the key held by the customer, a journal of every call, behaviour policies the agents cannot skip, cost per workload visible before the invoice, and an item taken off the top of the register. 'It is in Europe now' is not a decision somebody can defend. For an operator in Romania, Portugal or the UK, 'move to us' sells risk; 'keep your code, point it at us, and come out with versions, encryption, a journal and policies' sells value with the risk removed.

sources.where: The reason to move is never sovereignty; The business model

ideas.notes: A selling lesson in general form: find the return that closes before the risk does, and the buyer who owns that register line rather than the cloud bill. The article says its value list is 'still a little invisible to a signer' and needs sharpening; the business model's numbers are labelled assumptions, shapes not quotes, for somebody else to run. The margin is in the twin layer (journal, policy enforcement, reports a regulator or insurer accepts), not in storage and compute, which are commodities: the same reading as why-i-love-wardley-maps.

ideas.title: A villager move: no new features while you move, or nobody can tell which change broke what
ideas.statement: A migration is a pure villager move, from explorer to town planner: take something that works and make it boring, reliable and cheap, without changing what it does. The temptation to add features during it is the moment everything derails, because the migration is now also a product change and nobody can tell which of the two broke what. The argument that the move is what allows the features is right, and it is exactly why the two must not be mixed: move first, with the code unmodified and the twin adding its value underneath, then add the features the move made possible.

sources.where: A villager move: no new features

ideas.notes: The same rule the newsroom used for its own explorer-to-villager move (green-does-not-mean-live cites it): same bytes and same bugs first, features after. Could sit in shipped-means-the-user-has-it instead.

ideas.title: Every piece of software should run, unmodified, against a twin of every service it depends on
ideas.statement: If the application cannot tell a twin from the real service, the same unmodified code can run against an in-memory twin in milliseconds on a laptop, against a twin replaying last week's production journal, against a twin injecting the failures staging never shows (a timeout, a throttle, a permission that disappears halfway through a job), and against the real service for the final check. Most teams test against mocks they wrote themselves and hope production behaves the same; with twins the environment becomes a setting rather than a guess. Software that can only run against one provider's live API is software you cannot test properly, cannot move, and cannot put a policy in front of.

The twin is also where the journal and the behaviour policy live, because every call passes through it (mandate-reach-gap, one-way-two-way-doors). The 2018 Chaos Engineering outline is the failure-injection half of this.

ideas.title: The desktop is the barrier, not the model: prompt injection is not solved, so the box has to hold
ideas.statement: Anthropic's own measurements of prompt injection in browser use went from a 23.6% attack success rate without mitigations to 11.2% in August 2025 and to about 1% in November 2025, a rate that in their words 'still represents meaningful risk'; Brave showed in October 2025 that nearly invisible text in screenshots could hijack agentic browsers; OpenAI wrote that it is unlikely ever to be fully solved. A desktop shows an agent pages, documents and emails written by other people, so over a working month the question is not whether a page will try but what the agent can do when one succeeds. An egress allowlist limits where it can send, a box without secrets limits what it can send, a revocable identity limits for how long, a recording says what happened; the model's defences reduce how often that matters and do not replace it. One mandate per task, written before the desktop exists, and the desktop configured from it.

ideas.notes: The nine properties of a locked-down agent desktop: isolation, an egress allowlist, secrets kept outside, an identity of its own, a live view and takeover, a record, a clean reset, billing that follows the work, the right desktop. On 7 October 2026 every one could be bought somewhere and no single product had all nine; the three that stop a hijacked agent doing damage (allowlist, secrets outside, own identity) were documented on one product, with two of them in private beta there. The OpenAI quote is from news coverage. Extends mandate-reach-gap and not-on-your-laptop with the desktop case.

ideas.title: A read-only vault needs no code; a read-write vault server is 83 lines on a free plan
ideas.statement: Because the sgit server never sees a key or a plaintext byte, it has almost nothing to do, and that is what the test showed on 18 October 2026. Read-only: no code at all; sgit publish writes a folder any static host can serve, and the real client cloned it back identically. Read-write: one Worker of 83 lines, one R2 bucket and one Durable Object per vault, all on Cloudflare's free plan, run in Cloudflare's own runtime locally with the real client: create, push, clone; a stale push that merged; two pushes at once where one was told nothing was overwritten; a read-only clone that refused to write; a wrong write key answered 403; and no plaintext anywhere in what the server stored. It has not yet run on a real account, does not do files over 4 MB, and has one shared access token.

A nuance for the book's 'no servers of mine with logic in them': the 83 lines are logic of yours, the small commodity function the no-server article allows for the one real limit (writes that must be checked). The Worker and its wrangler configuration are printed in full in the article, so the weekend chapter can point at them rather than reprint them.

ideas.title: Reach is a computed value, and new capability lands as excess, never as new authority
ideas.statement: What an agent can reach is not a document but the output of a calculation, so the question to answer is what calculates it and whether that is a one-time snapshot or wired to the pipeline. When a connector or integration is added the reach grows, the gap recomputes and a re-review follows; the mandate is locked business logic that changes only through change control, so a new capability can only land in the gap as excess, never as new authority. Unbounded includes volume: an agent permitted £10k per action that can perform a thousand actions carries a £10m exposure.

ideas.title: Who can pull the plug: an agent that cannot be stopped is riskier than one that can
ideas.statement: Most AI projects do not fail technically; they stall when the business finally asks the good questions: can you stop it, what if it issues ten thousand of something, who is liable. Every board asks the same question about an agent in one sentence, who can pull the plug, how fast, what breaks and what cannot be undone, and a deployed agent's risk cannot be denied, only accepted by a named owner for an interval with an expiry. An agent that cannot be stopped is far riskier than one that can; containment (terminate, revoke, block, quarantine, ticket) is designed in advance and executed by the company's own stack.
