Quote worth keeping: 'The value is the support, not the code, so the code can stay open.' The ten-questions article calls the moat 'delivery, maintenance and trust', not lock-in.

ideas.title: Answer the hard questions in full, publish what is live and what is design, and check your own site against the answers
ideas.statement: When a buyer's, investor's or competitor's hard questions come back from a conference, answer them in one structured interview with an agent acting as a journalist that challenges every answer until the set holds together; publish an honest maturity table of what is live and what is design; and check the answers against what the company has already published. The exercise found three contradictions on RiskMandate's own site: a homepage saying 'enforced in real time', an insurance page in the present tense for things that were design, and a Level 1 price of £10 on two pages and £5 on a third.

sources.where: Where this comes from; Honest maturity, across all ten; Three things this exercise showed we must fix on our own site

ideas.notes: Could also sit in facts-and-the-record; placed in sell because the questions are a buyer's. The line that closes the set: 'Where we are early, we say so.'

ideas.title: A third input: a behaviour policy beside the system prompt and the prompt, which the vendor acknowledges, enforces where it can and answers for
ideas.statement: An agent today gets a system prompt from its vendor and a prompt from us; it should also take an Agent Behaviour Policy, written to a published standard, which the vendor accepts as part of the deployment, enforces as far as the platform can see, reports every breach against the same day and, eventually, carries liability for the rows it accepted. The user answers for what is outside the policy and the vendor for what is inside it, which is a better model than the user being liable for everything because they clicked allow. Most agents already run a hidden policy of their own (Claude in Chrome will not type a password), and a system prompt is a light behaviour policy not written as one; the layering is the vendor's published policy, then the deployer's, with the business logic only the deployer can write.

sources.where: The idea: a policy beside the prompt; The user answers outside the policy, the vendor inside it; A system prompt is a light behaviour policy; Most agents already run a policy

ideas.notes: A proposal: the article says no vendor accepts a behaviour policy as an input today in this sense; Claude Code's permission rules and managed settings are the nearest thing and cover settings, not business rules. Liability per row is the end state, not the start; acknowledgement and breach reporting can come first.

ideas.title: Models do not separate code from data, so a rule in the prompt can be argued with by an email
ideas.statement: In a computer the instructions and the data they operate on are kept apart, and most of the worst security bugs in history, from buffer overflows to SQL injection, are what happens when that separation breaks; in a language model there is no separation to break, every instruction and every piece of content arrives in the same channel, and the UK's National Cyber Security Centre said in December 2025 that prompt injection may never be mitigated the way SQL injection was. A behaviour policy does not fix this; it moves the most important instructions, what the agent may do, into a channel the content cannot reach, loaded by the platform, versioned, signed and checked outside the model where it can be.

sources.where: The old problem: code and data in one channel; What this does not claim

ideas.notes: Sits beside secrets-never-in-the-chat (the lethal trifecta) and is the reason mandate-reach-gap calls a rule in a prompt hope. Quote worth keeping, Simon Willison's: 'LLMs follow instructions in content'.

ideas.title: Aviation and payments got safe when the rule, the liability and the business model pointed the same way
ideas.statement: Aviation did not get safe out of altruism but because every crash became news: at 1995's rate of 2.72 fatal airliner accidents per million flights, 2025's 38.7 million flights would have meant about 105 fatal accidents; there were 12. Payments got some of the best security teams anywhere because the liability was moved onto the companies: a US cardholder liable for at most $50 since 1970, £35 in the UK, the 2015 liability shift onto whoever had not adopted chip cards, the PCI council founded by the card brands in 2006, and UK banks reimbursing scam victims up to £85,000 since October 2024, after which losses fell by around 21%. Regulation alone does not do it (Meta's €1.2 billion GDPR fine in 2023, €200 million in 2025); the improvement comes where a rule, a liability that lands on the company and a systemic risk to the business model line up, and agents can be that case.

sources.where: Aviation did not get safe out of altruism; Payments got safe because liability moved; Regulation alone does not do it

ideas.notes: The article's own caveats: the aviation numbers mix sources (Aviation Safety Network via Our World in Data, the Flight Safety Foundation, IATA); the 21% fall is one evaluation's estimate; 'it does not take many users' to lose trust in agents is Dinis's judgement with no number behind it.

ideas.title: Zoom into an agent's behaviour policy and you find the business logic, which only the business can write
ideas.statement: The first rules anybody writes for an agent are mechanical and the same in every company: do not send, only draft; do not delete; use your own account. A few questions in (which drafts may it send, can it mention a price, can it chase an invoice finance has not approved, can it write to a client in dispute) you are describing the business, in layers with different owners: the function, the process, the relationship, and what the company is for. Vendors stop at the mechanics by the shape of the problem, since a vendor that models each customer's business becomes a consultancy; the business layers are the customer's to write, and written together with skills (a skill says how, a policy layer says what is allowed, who owns the rule and what stands in the way) they are the business codified for an agent, which is what lets a company hand it real work and scale.

sources.where: Above the mechanics is the business; Why the vendors stop at the mechanics; It looks a lot like a skill

ideas.notes: The article's own five readers flag that its front matter overstates the body: 'the only way to describe agent behaviour at the granularity a business actually runs at' is unsupported; the body says only that a fractal structure is the one Dinis found that can hold it. The register should not say 'only way'. The firm, its rules and its counts are fictional on purpose.

ideas.title: Software was the law: the rule the screen enforced by omission is no longer enforced once an agent calls the API
ideas.statement: Companies never wrote their business logic down because they did not need to: a clerk could not send an unapproved invoice because the finance system had no button for it until the approval was recorded, and a support agent could not see payment details because their role did not include the screen. An agent works through APIs, not screens, and can call the endpoint the button would have called, so the rule the user interface enforced by omission is no longer enforced unless somebody writes it down and something enforces it; the behaviour policy is where it gets written down.

sources.where: Software was the law

ideas.notes: The Historian's reading of the article calls this its nugget: 'every later article is about the "something enforces it" half.' Approval chains, RBAC, field-level permissions and workflow engines are where privacy decisions and much of practical governance live.

ideas.title: Every rule lands in one of three states: backed by a control, governed by an accepted risk, or resting on hope
ideas.statement: For each rule the policy records what stands in the way: nothing, an expectation (a rule in prose, enforced by nobody), a setting the agent's own account can flip, or a boundary enforced above it, and only the boundary is a control. Add one more fact, whether a named person has accepted the risk of the rule not being enforced, with an expiry, and every rule is a control, an accepted risk or hope, which can be counted. In the article's fictional firm 5 of 17 rules are backed by a control, 6 by an accepted risk and 6 by hope; the platform layer is all control, the organisation layer all hope, and each existing product (a send gateway, an outbound content check, a blocked-recipients list) moves one row.

sources.where: How much of it is hope?; Where the vendors plug in

ideas.notes: Adds the third state, accepted risk, to mandate-reach-gap's hope versus enforcement. The proportions are illustrative; the article says the shape is the point. Resting on hope is not a failure, most of a business has always run on people behaving as asked, but with an agent it can be counted.

ideas.title: Open source is not free: somebody pays, and the people who get the value have no easy way to
ideas.statement: Somebody is paying for open source, even if only with their time. The long tail is measurable and not small: 6.99% of Homebrew's macOS install events in the last 30 days, and 16.66% over a year, came from versions older than the newest three, and 18.55% of pip downloads run on end-of-life Python. Money flows to old versions when a vendor owns them (Oracle earned $19.8 billion from support last year; Red Hat's subscriptions ran at about 93% gross margin) and not when a community does: open source receives about 0.09% of its estimated value in investment, and 60% of maintainers describe themselves as unpaid hobbyists. The question was never whether somebody pays; it is whether the people who get the value have an easy way to pay for it.

sources.where: In short; The long tail, measured; Where the money flows

ideas.notes: The case that started it: an Intel iMac clean-installed with macOS 13 for Dinis's agents could not run Homebrew or Docker Desktop and needed Python by hand; the research corrected the story (only the 2017 iMacs stop at Ventura; Homebrew now refuses the CPU, not just the OS). The xz maintainer wrote 'this is an unpaid hobby project' two years before the backdoor.

ideas.title: Below about five pounds the card fee is the price, so pence payments only work aggregated
ideas.statement: Stripe's standard UK rate is 1.5% plus 20p: on a £20 payment that is 2.5%, on £5 it is 5.5%, on 50p it is 41.5%, and on 10p it is more than the payment. So payments of pence only work aggregated: one charge a year that covers many projects, or a platform that already holds a balance and settles in bulk, which is how the newsroom's reading meter prices a page at a few pence against £5 of credit settled as one balance. Payment also has to be tied to a verified user who receives something, not to a count: when tea.xyz rewarded package popularity with tokens, one developer published nearly 14,000 packages.

sources.where: The pence problem; Why not just charge?, Per-install rewards get gamed

ideas.notes: The article finds the card-versus-platform difference smaller than expected at £2 to £3, where the 20p fee is under 10%; aggregation matters below about £1.

ideas.title: 'Nobody knows how it is built' is fixable: make the agents leave a record, a mandate, a memory and a graph
ideas.statement: HBR's warning that the AI designs the architecture so nobody in-house knows how the tool is built is true of most agent-built software today and does not have to be. If the agents work under a written mandate, keep their memory in a versioned store the company owns, and describe what they built as a graph, the architecture is a record the next team can read, not a mystery. A prototype ready for the villagers looks like Mondweep Chakravorty's SGit and Ruflo run: versions pinned, sixteen tests, a folder of evidence, a written behaviour policy, and a README that says plainly what it does not do yet.

sources.where: 'Nobody knows how it is built' can be fixed

ideas.notes: The article says the record is a proposal, not a standard: this site runs it; few organisations do yet. Dinis declares a stake: his companies sell open source and this kind of record.

ideas.title: The bonus test: if nobody will put their name or their bonus on it in production, it is not ready to be in line
ideas.statement: HBR's test for a chief executive, would your team accept a bonus tied to how this tool performs in production, is the town planner's accountability by another name: the moment someone takes the code and answers for it. The industry already says whoever ships code is responsible for it however it was written: the Linux kernel's rules say AI agents must not add Signed-off-by tags and only humans can certify the Developer Certificate of Origin, and Fedora's proposal says the contributor is always the author and fully accountable. An explorer cannot be made accountable for code they never read; the team the work is handed to can, and the town planners above all.

sources.where: The bonus test is accountability
Villagers and town planners

ideas.title: What the newsroom says about Lithuania and the Portuguese company, as of 12 October 2026: two lines
ideas.statement: The company Dinis created in Portugal for MyFeeds is being closed, because running a company with little revenue in Portugal is expensive in a way it is not in England; he is looking at Lithuania for the next one, for its digital advantages. The article's own limit: the company move is a consideration, not a decision; Lithuania is being looked at and nothing has been registered.

sources.where: The line that runs back, last paragraph; What this does not claim, 'The company move is a consideration, not a decision'

ideas.notes: This is all the newsroom has on Lithuania and on the Portuguese company. It is the evidence behind the Lithuania and Portugal lines of the-company-itself-for-real until the journalist's gap articles arrive; the book should not say more than this from this source.

ideas.title: The thinking is never wasted: pause in the open and pick up when the moment comes
ideas.statement: The Cyber Boardroom, a GenAI platform for boards with an advisor called Athena, taught Dinis what personas and customised output are worth and paused because nobody wants confidential board material in an environment somebody else runs; what it needed is what he later built as sgit. MyFeeds built personalised feeds on semantic graphs, found the industry silent on graphs, micropayments and paying the people who write, and paused. The 2025 writing on monetising trust, fact provenance and micro and nano payments is what the newsroom now stands on, and he is going back to the publishers with an end-to-end example; if it does not land in 2026 he will try in 2027. Because it was open and written down, it was there when the moment came.

sources.where: The line that runs back; Going back, with something that works; The thinking is never wasted

ideas.notes: The Cyber Boardroom and MyFeeds are summarised from memory in the article, and the proofs of concept are not all published. For the founder it illustrates connect-the-dots-backwards: a pivot leaves assets when it is done in the open.

ideas.title: Your own newsroom is the public example of your product, and underneath it a CRM and a publishing workflow
ideas.statement: The hardest part of selling behaviour policies and licences to operate is showing them in action, because customer work cannot be shared; the ecosystem around the newsroom, its agents, their behaviour policy, the status report every few answers, the leak scan before every commit, the releases with their logs, is the best public example RiskMandate has of a policy under real load every day. And a very effective newsroom is, underneath, a very effective CRM and publishing workflow: agents that follow up people and threads, draft, publish and keep a record, matured by readers in a way the product's own volumes could not yet force. Follow the users and the feedback loops, even when the user is you.

sources.where: The newsroom is RiskMandate's workflow, and its example; Why the newsroom could solve it and RiskMandate could not

ideas.notes: RiskMandate's traction is described, not measured, in the article.

ideas.title: An explorer-coded app is a brief, not a product: not ready to be in line, and the further towards commodity the fewer agents in line
ideas.statement: An explorer-coded app may look and feel like an application, but nobody has read the code or validated the architecture, so it is not ready to be in line, in the path of work other people depend on. Dependence comes quickly: once something is used it is mission critical, even for one person if it replaced how they work, and from then on new versions cannot break it. The direction is set by where the code sits on the map: the further towards commodity, the fewer agents in line and the more deterministic the code; a model has no place in line on a mission-critical path.

sources.where: Not ready to be in line; Villagers and town planners

ideas.notes: Pairs with the-handover (the move itself) and the-bonus-test-is-accountability (who answers for it). 'A model has no place in line on a mission-critical path' is quoted in the article from Dinis's code review piece.

ideas.title: Every product needs an explorer version, with paid conversions to a villager product and a town planner one
ideas.statement: Products need an explorer version in which users talk to the product with a model, reshape it, move things around and keep their own version, the product treated as primitives. When a user has something they want to keep they submit it, which is the brief, and pay to convert it into a villager product maintained across releases and, if it matters enough, a town planner product built properly or kept as a maintained fork. Each step is a revenue stream and each submission tells the vendor exactly what its users want; the same path should exist inside companies, between a department and its engineers, and around open-source projects, between users and maintainers.

sources.where: An explorer version of every product

ideas.notes: A proposal: the article knows of no vendor selling it. Could also sit in price-it-then-give-it-away as a pricing model; placed in the handover chapter because it is the handover, sold.

ideas.title: Write down what your agent can reach in twenty minutes: list its tools, say what you wanted it for, write the gap
ideas.statement: Few people have seen the list for their own agents. Paste the thirteen prompts from RiskMandate's try-it page into the assistant you already have connected to your mail: the first asks it to list its own tools ('the list is longer than the tile that sold it'), the second asks it to draft what you actually wanted it for in three lists, wanted, refused, never mentioned ('the correction is almost always downward'), the third writes the gap down. About twenty minutes, and nothing is collected. It is a self-report, the cheapest evidence there is and the weakest; a measured policy marks each row as measured, documented or inferred.

sources.where: Yes, it reports what an agent can actually do; How does it get into the room?, Twenty minutes

ideas.notes: A candidate for the hands-on part if a chapter on a first behaviour policy is added; none of the hands-on chapters covers it today. The paid levels are offerings, not a track record: the pricing page marks the £500 and £1,500 levels 'specified, never run' as of 15 September 2026.

ideas.title: Do not sell the need; answer a question somebody already has to answer, with a deadline
ideas.statement: There are two groups, the people who see how fast agents are moving and the much larger group who do not, and the second group will not ask for an agent risk tool because they do not see the risk. The way in is a question somebody already has, with a deadline, in the language of the room: a contract, where legal and procurement ask what a vendor's agent will do with the data; a security questionnaire, where a startup's first serious enterprise customer asks which agents touch their data and how they are bounded; an insurance renewal, where the question is whether AI is excluded from cover; the board's risk appetite; and twenty minutes with the assistant you already run. None of these asks anyone to understand agents first.

sources.where: How does it get into the room?

ideas.notes: A founder is on both sides: as the seller, and as the startup that, in the article's words, will be diligenced on its agents before long. The insurance argument is RiskMandate's, summarised from its pages, not independently surveyed.

ideas.title: The opportunity for a small country is the plumbing, built once by the state like a road, not the race for GPUs
ideas.statement: Frontier models, GPUs and data centres sit at the commodity end of the map with a lead a small country cannot buy back, so it should not enter that race. What stops a talented person in Braga or Cluj selling a service to the world is not talent, energy or price but forming a company, hiring across a border, being paid across Europe, working in another language, a contract, an invoice, a tax form, each custom built every time in most of Europe when it should be infrastructure the state built once, like the road the shop did not pay for. In 2021, 18.5% of EU enterprises sold online to customers in their own country, 8.1% to other EU countries and 4.6% to the rest of the world. Estonia built the road: more than 142,000 e-residents and more than 43,000 companies, over 4,200 of them founded in 2026 by mid-September, on X-Road, open source under the MIT licence and connecting around a thousand organisations.

sources.where: The race you cannot win, and should not enter; The opportunity is the plumbing; Infrastructure is the state's job

ideas.notes: Sharpens hack-your-country's 'judo for small countries' into the claim itself. The article says it is not a national strategy, the Eurostat figure is for 2021, and Estonia is a case study, not a template. For the founder it is the other side of the-company-itself: the plumbing a founder in the EU still builds alone.

ideas.title: No sovereignty without open source and open schemas; what the state pays for belongs to the commons; buy the alternative before the day you need it
ideas.statement: Sovereignty means you can leave: a road with a toll gate owned by one company is lock-in with tarmac, and independence is the ability to run a parallel service, move the data and keep going, which exists only if the code and the schemas are open. What the public paid for should be available to the public, not so everyone changes the production system but so everyone can see it, run it and leave with their data, which is also how the local industry around it comes into being. And a market for the alternative does not appear on the day the single point of failure fails: run parallel services, buy the local or open alternative for part of the estate now and accept fewer features, and use procurement, the lever a state already holds, to prefer open schemas and data mobility.

sources.where: Why it has to be open source; Create the demand before the day you need it; The playbook

ideas.notes: The five-move playbook: map the attrition, commoditise the plumbing, create the demand, put the money where the market is genesis, regulate what settled, then map again. hack-your-country already cites sovereignty-is-the-ability-to-move for the test; this is the civic argument behind it, and the resilience case rather than an ideological one.

ideas.title: Smaller models, more of them, with the least agency: a public model is a public road, and constraints are the input
ideas.statement: Most work does not need a frontier model and should not use one: frontier models are for finding the art of the possible, and for things that have to work every day at a price they are too expensive, too much power for the task and dangerous in proportion; the right end state uses the model once to build the tool, and production is plain files and plain code with no prompt in the path, with agents given the least agency that does the job. The market still at genesis is small open models for each language and culture, the Portuguese of Portugal, Brazil, Angola, Cape Verde and Mozambique, not one Portuguese; Portugal released Amalia on 1 July 2026, built by a consortium of universities with 5.5 million euros of EU recovery money and published with its dataset and code under an open licence. Constraints are the input: DeepSeek's V3 was trained in 2.788 million GPU hours on export-restricted H800 chips, and the constraint produced the innovation.

sources.where: Smaller models, more of them; Constraints are the input

ideas.notes: 'The model is used once to build the tool, and production is plain files and plain code' is also a building principle for ship-now-ship-serverless and not-ready-to-be-in-line. The DeepSeek example is about constraint, not cost: the dollar figure is disputed and the article does not rely on it.

ideas.title: What spending millions on Upwork taught: build the infrastructure first, and the jobs can go back to where people came from
ideas.statement: As a CISO and CTO Dinis spent millions on Upwork across the open source projects and the teams he ran, and it was one of the most successful things they did: distributed teams, people as good as or better than those hired the ordinary way, delivered faster and more efficiently. It worked because they invested first in the infrastructure around it, a project management team, a structure team and an onboarding team, and then used Upwork to manage Upwork, so the internal teams carried no overhead. It was never buying the cheapest: it was the right talent at a price fair where they lived, good value for both sides and a real career for the person. A small country that builds the plumbing makes the jobs available everywhere inside it, so people can go back to where the family and the lifestyle are; Romania's technology sector is close to 8% of GDP with more than 250,000 professionals and over ten billion euros a year of service exports.

sources.where: What I learned spending millions on a distributed workforce

ideas.notes: The Upwork spend and outcomes are Dinis's own and not independently verifiable from the article. Answers the 2018 Upwork outline from the hiring side rather than the freelancer's.
